snapshots.label: 1360 BC

cities.name: Thebes
cities.blurb: Egypt's capital at the height of the 18th Dynasty. Amenhotep III built on an unprecedented scale here: the Luxor temple, the Avenue of Sphinxes to Karnak, and on the west bank his vast mortuary temple and the Malkata palace-city.

image.description: The southern Colossus of Memnon (Luxor, Egypt)
image.caption: The southern Colossus of Memnon, one of two giant statues of Amenhotep III at the gateway of his mortuary temple at Thebes; photo 2011.

cities.name: Hattusa
cities.blurb: Hittite capital, with temples in its inner city and a royal acropolis on the Büyükkale ridge. Soon after this date Suppiluliuma I (c. 1344–1322 BC) ringed the inner and outer city with over 6 km of walls.

image.description: Lion Gate, Hattusa, Turkey
image.caption: The Lion Gate in the walls of Hattusa, near Boğazkale, Turkey; photo 2014.

cities.name: Dur-Kurigalzu
cities.blurb: A new royal city founded early in the 14th century BC by the Kassite king Kurigalzu I, who ruled Babylonia from here. It had a ziggurat to Enlil and appeared on toponym lists in Amenhotep III's Egyptian temple.

image.file: 1. The remains of the Kassite ziggurat at Aqar-Quf (Dur-Kurigalzu), western Baghdad, Iraq.jpg

cities.name: Mycenae
cities.blurb: Around this time Mycenae's acropolis was ringed with massive 'Cyclopean' walls enclosing a palace with a columned megaron throne room. Egypt knew the city by name, and a scarab of Queen Tiye, wife of Amenhotep III, reached its citadel temple.

chandler.name: Thebes
chandler.blurb: Egypt's capital at the height of the 18th Dynasty. Amenhotep III built on an unprecedented scale here: the Luxor temple, the Avenue of Sphinxes to Karnak, and on the west bank his vast mortuary temple and the Malkata palace-city.

image.description: The southern Colossus of Memnon (Luxor, Egypt)

chandler.name: Hattusa
chandler.blurb: Hittite capital, with temples in its inner city and a royal acropolis on the Büyükkale ridge. Soon after this date Suppiluliuma I (c. 1344–1322 BC) ringed the inner and outer city with over 6 km of walls.

image.caption: The Lion Gate in the walls of Hattusa, near Boğazkale, Turkey; photo 2014.

snapshots.label: 650 BC

cities.name: Nineveh
cities.blurb: Capital of Ashurbanipal, who built its North Palace and gathered a great library of cuneiform tablets here. Sennacherib had laid out new streets, squares and his 'palace without a rival'. Nineveh was sacked in 612 BC.

cities.name: Linzi
cities.blurb: Capital of Duke Huan, whose minister Guan Zhong made Qi China's most powerful state with reforms including monopolies on salt and iron. In 667 BC the Zhou king named Huan hegemon, the first of the Five Hegemons.

image.description: Photograph of a model of the ancient city of Linzi in the Museum of the Qi State.
image.caption: Modern model of the ancient city of Linzi in the Museum of the Qi State; photo 2010.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Royal seat of the Eastern Zhou, whose court had moved here from Haojing around 770 BC. By now the Zhou kings held little real power over the rival states of the Spring and Autumn period.

cities.polity: Babylonia under Shamash-shum-ukin, in revolt against the Neo-Assyrian Empire
cities.blurb: Under siege. Shamash-shum-ukin, the Assyrian prince ruling Babylonia, rebelled against his brother Ashurbanipal in 652 BC. By 650 Assyrian forces were besieging Babylon, which suffered famine and disease before falling in 648.

cities.name: Kosambi
cities.blurb: Capital of the Vatsa kingdom, on the Yamuna upstream of its confluence with the Ganges. Tradition says a Kuru king founded it after floods destroyed Hastinapura, and excavated palace foundations here go back to the 8th century BC.

chandler.name: Miletus
chandler.blurb: A wealthy Ionian port that, from the seventh century BC, was planting colonies along the Black Sea, such as Sinope and Olbia. It was said to have founded more colonies than any other Greek city.

chandler.name: Sais
chandler.blurb: Seat of the new Saite dynasty. Psamtik I, who had fled to Nineveh and returned, was recognised as sole king and unified Egypt with Carian and Greek mercenaries sent by Gyges of Lydia.

snapshots.note: Assyria shaped much of this list: Ashurbanipal ruled from Nineveh, his army was besieging his rebel brother in Babylon, and Sais's Psamtik I had come to power in Egypt after Assyria drove out the Kushite kings.

snapshots.label: 430 BC

cities.name: Xiadu
cities.blurb: Lower Capital of the northern state of Yan, set in the Taihang foothills between the Beiyi and Zhongyi rivers for defence. Its eastern half held the palace, royal cemeteries and workshops casting iron, bronze and coins.

image.description: Roof tile-end with animal mask design from the Warring States Period, Yan State. Unearthed at Yanxiadu, Yixian, Hebei Province, 1958.
image.caption: Warring States roof-tile end with an animal-mask design, made in the state of Yan and excavated at Xiadu in 1958.

cities.name: Babylon
cities.blurb: Capital of the Persian satrapy of Babylonia and an administrative capital of the Achaemenid Empire, where Babylonian astronomy and mathematics revived. Herodotus described its moat and its huge walls cemented with bitumen.

image.description: Pergamon museum Ishtar Gate in Berlin
image.caption: Nebuchadnezzar's Ishtar Gate of Babylon, rebuilt from excavated glazed bricks in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin; photo 2019.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Still the Zhou royal capital, which had moved in 510 BC from Wangcheng to nearby Chengzhou. The Warring States period had just begun, and real power lay with the rival states.

cities.name: Linzi
cities.blurb: The Jiang dukes still reigned in Linzi, but the Tian clan held real power. Around 481 BC the Tian chief took control of most of Qi, leaving the monarch little beyond the capital and the land around Mount Tai.

cities.blurb: Capital of Persian-ruled Egypt since Cambyses took it in 525 BC. A permanent Persian garrison held the city near the palace of Apries, and Herodotus visited and described its monuments in this century.

snapshots.label: 200 BC

cities.name: Pataliputra
cities.blurb: Capital of the Maurya Empire in its last decades. The Greek envoy Megasthenes had described a long city beside the Ganges, ringed by a deep moat and a timber wall with 570 towers and 64 gates.

cities.name: Alexandria
cities.blurb: Capital of Ptolemaic Egypt, known for its Pharos lighthouse and its Great Library. Around 200 BC Aristophanes of Byzantium became the Library's fourth head, after Eratosthenes, who had calculated the Earth's circumference.

cities.blurb: A brand-new capital. Liu Bang settled his court here in 202 BC, building Changle Palace across the river from the ruined Qin capital, and two years later the vast Weiyang Palace. Work on the city walls started in 194 BC.

cities.name: Seleucia
cities.blurb: Founded around 305 BC by Seleucus I as his first capital, largely peopled from Babylon. The court later moved to Antioch, but Seleucia, on the Tigris and a Euphrates canal, remained one of the great Hellenistic cities.

cities.name: Xianyang
cities.blurb: The burned-out former Qin capital. Xiang Yu set it alight in 206 BC, destroying the royal library's banned books. Liu Bang's new Han capital, Chang'an, was rising just across the Wei River and would absorb Xianyang's southern parts.

chandler.name: Rome
chandler.blurb: Just victorious over Carthage, Rome was for the first time the capital of an overseas empire. From the 2nd century BC its population surged as Italian farmers, pushed off the land by slave-run estates, moved to the city.

chandler.name: Carthage
chandler.blurb: Defeated at Zama in 202 BC, Carthage accepted Roman peace terms that stripped its overseas territories and imposed a heavy indemnity. A grid-planned residential quarter on the Byrsa hill dates from about this time.

Chang'an only became the Han capital in 202 BC, so treat its ranking this year with caution. Not resolved without the book itself.

snapshots.label: 100 BC

cities.name: Alexandria
cities.blurb: Ptolemaic capital, with its Lighthouse, Serapeum and Museion. Ptolemy X had his mother Cleopatra III murdered in 101 BC and ruled with his niece-wife Berenice III until the Alexandrians expelled him in 88 BC.

image.description: A drawing of the Pharos of Alexandria by German archaeologist Prof. H. Thiersch (1909).
image.caption: Reconstruction drawing of the Pharos, the Lighthouse of Alexandria, by the German archaeologist Hermann Thiersch, 1909.

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: In 100 BC Marius, victor over the Cimbri, held his sixth consulship. When his ally the tribune Saturninus seized the Capitoline, Marius besieged him under a senatorial emergency decree, and a mob killed Saturninus in the senate house.

image.file: RRC 326.1 Gaius Fundanius depicting Gaius Marius triumphator.png
image.description: Obverse of RRC 326/1, a silver denarius by Gaius Fundanius in 101 BC depicting Gaius Marius as triumphator on quadriga
image.caption: Silver denarius of the moneyer Gaius Fundanius, 101 BC, showing Marius as triumphator in a four-horse chariot.

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: Emperor Wu's palace-building peaked around 100 BC; by the end of his reign, palaces filled two-thirds of the walled city. After Zhang Qian's missions west, Chang'an was the eastern terminus of the Silk Road.

image.file: Round eave tile with cloud design, attributed to Weiyang Palace, Xi'an, Shaanxi province, China, Western Han dynasty, 3rd-2nd century BC, ceramic - Tokyo National Museum - Tokyo, Japan - DSC08507.jpg

image.caption: Round ceramic eave tile with a cloud design attributed to Chang'an's Weiyang Palace, Western Han, 3rd-2nd century BC; Tokyo National Museum.

cities.name: Seleucia
cities.blurb: Founded as the first Seleucid capital, it fell to the Parthian king Mithridates I in 141 BC and became Parthia's western capital. It stayed a Hellenistic city, and its mint struck Parthia's first tetradrachms.

image.file: Tetradrachm of Mithridates II of Parthia, minted at Seleucia between 120 and 109 BC.jpg
image.description: Tetradrachm of Mithridates II of Parthia, minted at Seleucia between 120 and 109 BC.
image.caption: Silver tetradrachm of the Parthian king Mithridates II, minted at Seleucia between 120 and 109 BC.

cities.name: Antioch
cities.blurb: Seleucid royal capital on the Orontes, a four-quartered Tetrapolis. Its citizens took sides in the dynasty's feuds, and in 83 BC they turned on their feeble kings and invited Tigranes the Great to occupy the city.

image.description: The Tyche (Fortune) of Antioch. Marble, Roman copy after a Greek bronze original by Eutychides of the 3rd century BC.
image.caption: The Tyche (Fortune) of Antioch, the city's patron goddess; Roman marble copy of a 3rd-century BC Greek bronze by Eutychides, Vatican Museums.

snapshots.note: Alexander's successor kingdoms were in decline: the Parthians had taken Mesopotamia from the Seleucids, and Rome would absorb Seleucid Syria in 64 BC and, after Actium, Ptolemaic Egypt.

snapshots.label: AD 1

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: Augustus was turning Rome from brick to marble. His Forum, with its Temple of Mars Ultor, had been inaugurated in 2 BC, and his grandson and adopted heir Gaius was consul for AD 1.

image.file: Forum of Augustus, Temple of Mars Ultor 2013.jpg

image.caption: Remains of the Temple of Mars Ultor in the Forum of Augustus, Rome; photo 2013.

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: The Han capital, where Wang Mang ruled as regent for the boy Emperor Ping. In AD 1 he was made Duke of Anhan, 'Duke who made Han secure', the first duke in Han history.

image.description: Site of front hall of Weiyang Palace in Chang'an city of Han Dynasty(Western, 206 BC – 9 AD)
image.caption: Rammed-earth foundations of the front hall of the Weiyang Palace, the Han emperors' palace in Chang'an; photo 2013.

cities.name: El Mirador

sources: hucs:El Mirador, the Lost City of the Maya

cities.blurb: The great Preclassic Maya centre, crowned by triadic pyramids such as La Danta, with raised white causeways running to Nakbe and El Tintal. It would be abandoned by about AD 150.

image.caption: The La Danta pyramid at El Mirador, Guatemala; photo 2007.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: The old Zhou royal city, where the Han founder first ruled before choosing Chang'an, was now the seat of Henan Commandery. Wang Mang would put one of his six state market offices here in AD 10.

image.description: Tomb Museum, Luoyang, Henan Province. Complete indexed photo collection at WorldHistoryPics.com.
image.caption: A painted Western Han brick tomb, reassembled in the ancient tombs museum at Luoyang; photo 2007.

snapshots.note: Two great empires spanned Eurasia: Augustus's Rome, early in the two-century Pax Romana, and Han China, where the regent Wang Mang would seize the throne in AD 9.

snapshots.label: AD 100

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: Trajan, who entered Rome as emperor in 99, opened his third consulship here on 1 January 100. He was rebuilding the Circus Maximus, replacing wooden seating with stone; the work was finished by 103.

image.caption: The site of the Circus Maximus seen from the Palatine Hill, Rome; photo 2014.

cities.blurb: Eastern Han capital of Emperor He, who in 92 closed the city gates and overthrew the Dou clan, leaning on palace eunuchs. In the palace workshop the eunuch Cai Lun would improve papermaking in 105.

image.file: Eastern Han Luoyang Mural of Liubo players.jpg
image.description: Detail of a mural from an Eastern Han tomb at Zhucun 朱村, Luoyang 洛陽, Henan province. The two figures in the foreground are playing Liubo, with the playing mat between them, and the Liubo board to the side of the mat. The two red, circular objects next to the liubo board are probably intended to represent lacquer wine cups. The player on the right is taking his turn, with his right hand raised up as if about to throw down the six throwing sticks. The mural is coloured using "Han Blue" and "Han Purple" pigments.
image.caption: Two men playing the board game liubo, detail of a mural from an Eastern Han tomb (AD 25-220) at Zhucun, Luoyang.

cities.name: Alexandria
cities.blurb: Capital of Roman Egypt, a province held by the emperor through his own prefect, and a key granary for Rome. Tension between Jews and Greeks had brought riots in AD 38 and 66.

image.file: Monete romane, alessandria, in bronzo, con faro e imbarcazione, II secolo dc. 01.jpg
image.description: coins in the Numismatic Museum of Athens
image.caption: Roman bronze coins of Alexandria showing the Pharos lighthouse and a ship, 2nd century AD; Numismatic Museum of Athens.

cities.name: Antioch
cities.blurb: Roman emperors treated it as an eastern Rome, adding a forum, colonnades and a hippodrome modelled on the Circus Maximus. It was a chief centre of early Christianity, where converts were first called Christians.

image.file: Mosaic of Isiac Ceremony, from Daphne near Antioch, 2nd century AD, Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya, Turkey (36063955161).jpg
image.credit: Mosaic of Isiac Ceremony, from Daphne near Antioch, 2nd century AD, Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya, Turkey
image.description: Depicting a ceremony for Isis who, in Ancient Egyptian legends, is the sister and wife of god-king Osiris and mother of Horus, god of the sun, this mosaic is largely damaged. The figure on the right of the mosaic holds in her hand one of the objects ascribed to Isis. The figure on the left has a hand in the air and wears a robe with crescent ornaments.
image.caption: Mosaic of a ceremony for Isis from Daphne, Antioch's suburb, 2nd century AD; Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya.

cities.name: Carthage
cities.blurb: Refounded by Julius Caesar as Colonia Iulia Concordia Carthago, it was the capital of grain-rich Roman Africa and the second city of the western empire. Its amphitheatre was built around this time.

image.file: Roman amphitheatre of Carthage - view from above.jpg
image.description: Amphithéâtre romain, Carthage
image.caption: The arena of the Roman amphitheatre of Carthage, Tunisia; photo 2010.

cities.name: Seleucia
cities.blurb: Under Parthian rule it was still, Tacitus wrote, a fully Hellenistic city, and the earliest Parthian iwans were built here in the early 1st century AD. Trajan would burn it in 117.

image.file: Tetradrachm of Vonones I, Seleucia mint.jpg
image.description: Tetradrachm of Vonones I, Seleucia mint.
image.caption: Silver tetradrachm of the Parthian king Vonones I (reigned AD 8-12), struck at the Seleucia mint.

snapshots.note: Rome and Han China were both near their height: Trajan would take the Roman Empire to its greatest extent in 117, while the restored Eastern Han ruled China from Luoyang.

snapshots.label: AD 200

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: Septimius Severus had replaced the Praetorian Guard with Danubian veterans and stationed a new legion at Albanum, 20 km away. After defeating Parthia he raised a triumphal arch in the Forum, and he also built the Septizodium.

image.file: Arch of Septimius Severus in Rome (1).jpg
image.description: Arch of Septimius Severus – Forum Romanum in Rome, Lazio, Italy
image.caption: The Arch of Septimius Severus in the Roman Forum, raised after his Parthian victory; photo 2018.

cities.name: Alexandria
cities.blurb: Egypt's grain came down the Nile to Lake Mareotis and sailed from Alexandria's Great Harbour for Rome. Clement ran the city's Catechetical School, teaching Christianity through Greek philosophy, until Septimius Severus's persecution drove him to Palestine in 202.

sources.title: Grain supply to the city of Rome - Wikipedia

image.file: Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa, Alexandria, Egypt.jpg
image.description: Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa, Alexandria, Egypt
image.caption: Relief of Anubis tending the dead in the Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa, tombs cut in the 2nd century AD and used into the 4th; photo 2020.

cities.name: Carthage
cities.blurb: Centre of Roman Africa, a breadbasket of the empire, with the seaside Baths of Antoninus, Africa's largest. Tertullian, the first theologian to write in Latin, worked here; in 203 Perpetua and Felicity were executed at games for Geta's birthday.

image.description: Baths of Carthage, located in Carthage, Tunisia
image.caption: Ruins of the Baths of Antoninus, built under Antoninus Pius on the shore at Carthage; photo 2014.

cities.name: Antioch
cities.blurb: Rome's emperors treated it as an eastern Rome, adding colonnades, baths, a granite-paved main street and a vast circus. The usurper Pescennius Niger, beaten by Septimius Severus in 194, was captured while fleeing from Antioch.

image.file: Mosaic of Isiac Ceremony, from Daphne near Antioch, 2nd century AD, Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya, Turkey (36063955161).jpg
image.credit: Mosaic of Isiac Ceremony, from Daphne near Antioch, 2nd century AD, Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya, Turkey
image.description: Depicting a ceremony for Isis who, in Ancient Egyptian legends, is the sister and wife of god-king Osiris and mother of Horus, god of the sun, this mosaic is largely damaged. The figure on the right of the mosaic holds in her hand one of the objects ascribed to Isis. The figure on the left has a hand in the air and wears a robe with crescent ornaments.
image.caption: Floor mosaic of a ceremony for Isis from Daphne, Antioch's garden suburb, made in the 2nd century AD; Hatay Archaeology Museum.

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: The old Western Han capital, where Dong Zhuo forced the Han court in 190. After Dong's murder his generals Li Jue and Guo Si feuded; Emperor Xian escaped east in 195, and the court now sat at Xu.

image.description: Site of front hall of Weiyang Palace in Chang'an city of Han Dynasty(Western, 206 BC – 9 AD)
image.caption: Site of the Front Hall of Weiyang Palace, the Han palace at Chang'an that the late Eastern Han court also used; photo 2013.

snapshots.note: In 200, with China splitting into warlord states, Cao Cao, who held the Han emperor at Xu, turned on his northern rival Yuan Shao, while Septimius Severus had restored peace to Rome after the upheavals of the late 2nd century.

snapshots.label: AD 300

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: No longer where emperors lived: the four tetrarchs ruled from frontier capitals such as Milan, leaving Rome the nominal capital under its own city prefect. Even so, the Baths of Diocletian, the largest imperial baths, were rising on the Viminal.

image.description: Cross-section of the Baths of Diocletian by French architect Edmond Paulin
image.caption: Cross-section reconstructing the Baths of Diocletian, built 298–306, drawn by the architect Edmond Paulin in 1880.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Capital of the Western Jin, which had reunited China in 280. In 300 its palace turned deadly: Empress Jia had the crown prince murdered, then Sima Lun deposed her and forced her suicide, deepening the War of the Eight Princes.

sources.title: War of the Eight Princes - Wikipedia

image.description: Prehistory to Sui Dynasty Gallery, New Luoyang City Museum, Henan, China. Complete indexed photo collection at WorldHistoryPics.com.
image.caption: Western Jin pottery warrior figure in the Luoyang Museum; photo 2014.

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: No longer a capital, Chang'an was the base of Sima Yong, Prince of Hejian, in the War of the Eight Princes. In 304 his general Zhang Fang brought Emperor Hui here, and in 306 Xianbei troops sacked the city.

sources.title: War of the Eight Princes - Wikipedia
War of the Eight Princes - Wikipedia
War of the Eight Princes - Wikipedia

cities.name: Xuchang
cities.blurb: Cao Cao's seat for the captive Han emperor from 196 and Cao Wei's first capital in 220, Xuchang was now a Western Jin military command. In 300 Sima Lun sent the resentful Prince of Qi, Sima Jiong, to hold it.

sources.title: War of the Eight Princes - Wikipedia

cities.name: Ye
cities.blurb: Cao Cao had rebuilt Ye after 204 in the mould of an imperial capital, adding the Bronze Bird Terrace in 210. In 299 the Prince of Chengdu, Sima Ying, was posted here, and Xianbei troops sacked the city in 304.

sources.title: War of the Eight Princes - Wikipedia

image.description: Site of the Bronze Bird Terrace
image.caption: Site of the Bronze Bird Terrace at Ye, raised by Cao Cao in 210; photo 2025.

snapshots.note: Diocletian's accession in 284 ended Rome's Crisis of the Third Century, and his Tetrarchy ruled from frontier capitals; China, reunited by the Western Jin in 280, was sliding into the civil War of the Eight Princes.

noteSources.title: Crisis of the Third Century - Wikipedia

snapshots.label: AD 361

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: Still formally a capital, but emperors now ruled from elsewhere. Rome kept its prestige: Constantine had given the Lateran Palace to the Pope and built Old St Peter's, while its senators remained a stronghold of paganism.

image.description: Arch of Constantine (Rome) ,lateral view
image.caption: The Arch of Constantine, erected to celebrate his victory over Maxentius; photo 2014.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Constantine's city, proclaimed the new capital of the Roman Empire in 330. His son Constantius II, who took the eastern provinces including Constantinople, died in November 361 on the brink of civil war with his cousin Julian.

image.description: Column of Constantine, Istanbul
image.caption: The Column of Constantine, completed around 328 for the city's dedication and still standing in Istanbul's Çemberlitaş district; photo 2018.

cities.name: Ctesiphon
cities.blurb: Capital of Shapur II, who renewed war on Rome in 359 and retook Singara and Amida. In 363 the emperor Julian would defeat Shapur's forces outside Ctesiphon but fail to take the city.

image.description: Palacio de Ctesifonte
image.caption: The Taq Kasra, the great arched hall of Ctesiphon's royal palace, drawn in 1824; its construction date, somewhere between the 3rd and 6th centuries, is disputed.

cities.name: Antioch
cities.blurb: Seat of the count of the East and a mixed pagan and Christian city, whose leading church was Constantine's Great Church, begun in 327. The next year Julian, on campaign against Persia, would clash bitterly with its citizens.

image.description: Part of the border of the Megalopsychia hunt mosaic from the latter half of the 5th century from Daphne (Yakto) that may show the Imperial Palace and Great Church of Antioch
image.caption: Detail from the border of the late 5th-century Megalopsychia mosaic from Daphne, thought to show Antioch's imperial palace and Great Church.

cities.name: Jiankang
cities.blurb: Capital of the Eastern Jin since 317, when Sima Rui made it his seat after northern China fell. Its palaces were rebuilt in 330–332, setting the city's layout, though it still had only bamboo stockades, not brick walls.

image.file: 20240604 Site of Jiankang in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum.jpg
image.description: Excavation site of Jiankang in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum
image.caption: Excavated remains of Six Dynasties Jiankang displayed in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum, Nanjing; photo 2024.

cities.name: Pataliputra
cities.blurb: Re-emerging as an important city under the Gupta dynasty, whose reputed capital it was, though historians debate this. The reigning king, Samudragupta, is praised on the Allahabad Pillar for wide conquests and as a poet and musician.

snapshots.label: AD 400

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: Emperor Honorius held court at Milan, not Rome. In 401, as Alaric's Visigoths entered Italy, Rome's walls and gates were improved and Hadrian's Tomb became a fortress; in 410 Alaric sacked the city anyway.

image.description: Southern part Aurelian Walls around of old Rome city near of Porta san Sebastiano in Italy
image.caption: Rome's Aurelian Walls near Porta San Sebastiano, the circuit Honorius improved in 401; photo 2011.

cities.name: Jiankang
cities.blurb: Capital of the Eastern Jin since 317. The regent Sima Yuanxian governed for the disabled Emperor An; late in 399 Sun En's rebels overran Yang Province and advanced on Jiankang, and soon after the warlord Huan Xuan took the city.

image.file: 20240604 Site of Jiankang in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum.jpg
image.description: Excavation site of Jiankang in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum
image.caption: Excavated remains of Jiankang displayed in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum, Nanjing; photo 2024.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Sacked by the Han-Zhao in 311 and fought over ever since, the former Jin capital changed hands again in winter 399, when Yao Xing's Later Qin forces took it and the surrounding cities from the Eastern Jin.

image.file: 20240815 Site of Luoyang City from Han to Wei Dynasty - Site of the Palace City 05.jpg
image.description: Site of the Palace City in the Site of Luoyang City from Han to Wei Dynasty
image.caption: Rammed-earth remains of the palace city at the site of Han–Wei Luoyang; photo 2024.

cities.name: Pingcheng
cities.blurb: Tuoba Gui made Pingcheng the Northern Wei capital in 398, after overrunning Later Yan, and proclaimed himself emperor in 399. He founded an imperial university here, had books gathered from across his realm, and resettled people deported from conquered lands.

image.caption: Northern Wei eave tiles with moulded inscriptions, displayed in the Datong Museum; photo 2025.

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: Capital of the Qiang-ruled Later Qin. Yao Xing invited Confucian scholars to teach here while heavily promoting Buddhism: the monk Faxian set out from Chang'an for India in 399, and Kumarajiva reached the court in 401 to translate Sanskrit texts.

cities.name: Ye
cities.blurb: A year-long siege in the 380s left Ye so ruined that the Later Yan ruled from Zhongshan instead. Around the new year 398 its defender Murong De abandoned it to Tuoba Gui, who briefly considered making Ye his capital.

sources.title: Emperor Daowu of Northern Wei - Wikipedia
Emperor Daowu of Northern Wei - Wikipedia

snapshots.note: Northern China was split among as many as nine states in 400, with the Eastern Jin ruling the south from Jiankang; a year later Alaric's Visigoths invaded Roman Italy.

snapshots.label: AD 500

votes.label: Early Medieval and Byzantine Civilization: Constantine to Cr

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, which flourished while the western half collapsed. The double line of the Theodosian Walls, built this century, now protected it, and for most of the Byzantine period it was Europe's largest city.

image.description: Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, Istanbul
image.caption: A surviving stretch of the 5th-century Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, Istanbul; photo 2017.

cities.name: Ctesiphon
cities.blurb: Kavad I had just regained his throne, returning to the capital in 498 with a Hephthalite army after nobles deposed him for backing Mazdak's egalitarian sect. Veh-Ardashir, the western district, was seat of the Nestorian patriarch.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei moved his capital here in 493 as part of his sinicization campaign. Work began on the Buddhist Longmen Grottoes, and the Yongning Temple pagoda, China's tallest, was built in the city.

image.caption: Cliffside Buddhist caves of the Longmen Grottoes near Luoyang, begun under the Northern Wei; photo 2019.

cities.name: Jiankang
cities.blurb: Capital of the Southern Qi. The city gained brick walls around 480 and hosted literary circles such as the Eight Friends of Jingling. Rebellions against Emperor Xiao Baojuan would soon bring Xiao Yan's Liang dynasty to power.

cities.name: Pingcheng
cities.blurb: After the Northern Wei court moved to Luoyang in 494, Pingcheng stayed a secondary capital and base of the conservative Xianbei military elite. At nearby Yungang, imperial cave-carving had ended, but private patrons kept cutting caves.

cities.blurb: Held by the Northern Wei since its Later Yan defender fled around 398, Ye was no longer a capital; Emperor Daowu had briefly considered making it one. Earlier it had been capital of the Later Zhao and Former Yan.

snapshots.note: The last Western Roman emperor had been deposed in 476, leaving Constantinople as the surviving Roman capital. China was split between the Northern Wei, ruling from Luoyang, and southern dynasties at Jiankang.

snapshots.label: AD 622

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: Only four years earlier Li Yuan had proclaimed the Tang dynasty here, renaming the Sui capital Daxing, laid out from 582 on a grid of walled wards, as Chang'an.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Heraclius's capital was under pressure: Persian conquests had cut its Egyptian grain supply, ending free bread in 618, and Avars threatened from the Balkans. In 626 it would withstand a joint Sasanian–Avar siege.

cities.blurb: Capital of Khosrow II's Sasanian Empire, a sprawling metropolis of several districts known in Arabic as al-Mada'in. In 627 the Byzantine emperor Heraclius would surround the city before the Persians accepted his peace terms.

image.file: The massive walls of the Cairo Citadel (14815621603).jpg
image.credit: The massive walls of the Cairo Citadel
image.description: The Saladin Citadel of Cairo is a medieval Islamic fortification in Cairo, Egypt. The location, on Mokattam hill near the center of Cairo, was once famous for its fresh breeze and grand views of the city. It is now a preserved historic site, with mosques and museums. The Citadel was fortified by the Ayyubid ruler Salah al-Din (Saladin) between 1176 and 1183 CE, to protect it from the Crusaders. Only a few years after defeating the Fatimid Caliphate, Saladin set out to build a wall that would surround both Cairo and Fustat. Saladin is recorded as saying, "With a wall I will make the two [cities of Cairo and Fustat] into a unique whole, so that one army may defend them both; and I believe it is good to encircle them with a single wall from the bank of the Nile to the bank of the Nile." The Citadel would be the centerpiece of the wall. Built on a promontory beneath the Muqattam Hills, a setting that made it difficult to attack, the efficacy of the Citadel's location is further demonstrated by the fact that it remained the heart of Egyptian government until the 19th century. The citadel stopped being the seat of government when Egypt's ruler, Khedive Ismail, moved to his newly built Abdin Palace in the Ismailiya neighborhood in the 1860s. While the Citadel was completed in 1183–1184, the wall Saladin had envisioned was still under construction in 1238, long after his death [Wikipedia.org]
image.caption: Walls of Saladin's Citadel of Cairo, begun in 1176; photographed in 2012.

image.file: Les Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry octobre.jpg
image.description: La scène paysanne du premier plan représente les semailles. À droite, un homme sème à la volée. Des pies et des corneilles picorent les graines qui viennent d'être semées, à proximité d'un sac blanc et d'une gibecière. Derrière, un épouvantail en forme d'archer et des fils tendus, sur lesquels sont accrochés des plumes, sont destinés à éloigner les oiseaux. À gauche, un paysan à cheval passe la herse sur laquelle est posée une pierre qui permet aux dents de pénétrer plus profondément dans la terre. Il recouvre ainsi les grains qui viennent d'être semés. À l'arrière-plan, le peintre a représenté le Palais du Louvre. Du château au centre, on distingue, outre le donjon central qui accueillait alors le trésor royal, la façade orientale à droite, encadrée par la tour de la Taillerie et la tour de la Chapelle, et à gauche la façade méridionale, avec ses deux tours jumelées au centre. L'ensemble est entouré d'une enceinte ponctuée de trois tours et de deux bretèches, visibles ici. Sur la rive, des personnages conversent ou se promènent.
image.caption: October page of the Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry, painted between 1412 and 1416, with the Louvre fortress behind the Seine.

cities.name: Beijing
cities.blurb: Ming capital since 1421, Beijing centred on the Forbidden City, built 1406–1420. Imperial granaries near the Grand Canal's terminus fed its people, who had switched to coal once the surrounding forests were cut down.

cities.name: Vijayanagara
cities.blurb: By 1500 Vijayanagara was probably India's richest city, drawing traders from Persia and Portugal. Power lay with the regent Tuluva Narasa Nayaka, who defended the empire against the Gajapati king and the Bahmani Sultan.

image.description: Vijaya Vitthala Temple, Hampi, Karnataka, India, reflected in a shallow pool filled with rainwater. The Vitthala temple and market complex is over 3 kilometres (1.9 miles) north-east of the Virupaksha temple near the banks of the Tungabhadra River. It is an artistically sophisticated Hindu temple in Hampi, and is part of the sacred centre of Vijayanagara.
image.caption: The Vitthala temple complex in the ruins of Vijayanagara at Hampi, photographed in 2019.

cities.name: Cairo
cities.blurb: Sultan Qaytbay (r. 1468–1496) had built or restored numerous monuments in Cairo, but after him the crisis of Mamluk power deepened, and a new sea route around Africa soon let spice traders bypass the city.

cities.name: Tenochtitlan
cities.blurb: Capital of the Mexica under Ahuitzotl, who more than doubled the lands under Aztec dominance. After a flood of Lake Texcoco he rebuilt the island city on a grander scale; in 1487 he had inaugurated an enlarged Templo Mayor.

cities.name: Beijing

image.description: "Departure Herald", 26 m (85 ft) in length, from the Jiajing reign period (1522-1566 AD); the painting shows the emperor's large procession heading towards the imperial tombs of the Ming emperors located roughly 50 km north of the capital Beijing. This painting is usually paired with another panoramic painting called "Return Clearing", 31 m (98 ft) in length, which shows the emperor returning to the capital from the tombs by river boat. From Paludan's source listed below, this passage describes a particular scene of this painting: "Detail of a silk scroll, The Emperor's Approach, showing the luxury in which the emperor Xuande travelled. Elephants were kept in the imperial elephant stables until around 1900 and were often used for ceremonial occasions, such as the emperor's visits to the Temple of Heaven. Here, however, the large number of horsemen accompanying the emperor's carriage suggests that the emperor was on a much longer journey in the countryside." Paludan, Ann. (1998). Chronicle of the Chinese Emperors: the Reign-by-Reign Record of the Rulers of Imperial China. London: Thames & Hudson Ltd. ISBN 0500050902. Page 177.

cities.blurb: Rebuilding was slow after so much housing was destroyed in the war, and the authorities were turning to high-rise flats to ease the shortage. The 1951 Festival of Britain on the South Bank would mark a new mood of optimism.

cities.name: Osaka
cities.blurb: Expo '70, the first world's fair held in Asia, ran from March to September 1970 in the Senri Hills at Suita, with a master plan led by Kenzō Tange and Tarō Okamoto's Tower of the Sun.

image.credit: originally posted to Flickr as Festival Plaza
image.description: Festival Plaza Osaka Expo'70. An electric Daihatsu "Pavillion Car" can be seen in the center.
image.caption: The Festival Plaza at Expo '70, photographed 10 April 1970.

cities.name: Mexico City
cities.blurb: The 1968 Olympics, preceded by government troops' massacre of protesting students at Tlatelolco, were followed in 1969 by the first Metro line; through the 1970s smog and shanty towns grew faster than services.

image.description: mexican students on a burned bus
image.caption: Students on a burned bus during the protests in Mexico City, July 1968.

cities.name: Buenos Aires
cities.blurb: The city was torn by fighting between left-wing guerrillas and the right-wing Triple A; after the 1976 coup, the Dirty War's disappearances brought the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo to march silently.

image.description: colectivos on B. de Irigoyen street to Constitución station
image.caption: Colectivo buses on Bernardo de Irigoyen street, heading for Constitución station, in the 1970s.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: Japan's bubble economy sent Tokyo land prices soaring; developers replaced wooden houses with concrete high-rises in a loosely controlled boom that worsened traffic, until interest rates rose at the end of 1989.

image.description: 017 Shinjuku, Jan 82
image.caption: Shinjuku, Tokyo, photographed in January 1982.

cities.name: Osaka
cities.blurb: To revive a region losing ground to Tokyo, work began in 1987 on Kansai International Airport, built on an artificial island in Osaka Bay because the old Itami Airport was hemmed in by suburbs.

image.file: JA8150, Boeing 747-200 of Japan Airlines at Osaka International Airport, 1980's.jpg
image.credit: I scan the photograph which I photographed with MINOLTA single-lens reflex camera with a copier
image.description: It is the photograph which it photographed in Itami, Osaka Airport in 1980's.
image.caption: A Japan Airlines Boeing 747 at Osaka International (Itami) Airport in the 1980s.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: Mayor Ed Koch balanced the budget and ended the fiscal crisis by 1981, and a Wall Street boom fed property speculation, but the crack epidemic sent murders soaring and homelessness spread.

sources.title: History of New York City (1978–present) - Wikipedia

image.caption: 42nd Street in Manhattan, in disrepair in 1985 before its renovation.

cities.name: Mexico City
cities.blurb: On 19 September 1985 a magnitude 8.1 earthquake collapsed hundreds of buildings and killed thousands; many damaged tenements in the long-neglected historic centre were never rebuilt.

image.description: Mexico City Earthquake, September 19, 1985. Nuevo Leon fifteen-story reinforced concrete structure. Part of the building was only slightly damaged, while another part of it collapsed.
image.caption: The partly collapsed Nuevo León building after the earthquake of 19 September 1985.

cities.name: São Paulo
cities.blurb: As economic crisis eroded the military regime, the Diretas Já campaign for direct presidential elections held its first major rally on Praça da Sé in January 1984 and a vast final one in the Anhangabaú Valley that April.

image.description: Diretas Já rally in the city of São Paulo.
image.caption: Diretas Já rally in São Paulo, 16 April 1984.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: The bubble burst in the early 1990s, starting the 'Lost Decades' of stagnation. The new Metropolitan Government Building opened in 1991, and in 1995 the Aum Shinrikyo cult released sarin on the subway.

image.file: 【地下鉄サリン事件】除染を行う自衛隊員と警察官.jpg

image.description: Japan Ground Self-Defense Force troops (with dark-green clothing) and Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department officers (with white clothing) decontaminating the area at the Tokyo subway sarin attack.
image.caption: Soldiers and police decontaminating after the Tokyo subway sarin attack, 20 March 1995.

cities.name: Osaka
cities.blurb: Kansai International Airport opened on its artificial island in September 1994; in January 1995 the Great Hanshin earthquake devastated nearby Kobe, while the new airport came through unscathed.

image.description: Around Iwaya Intersection, National Route 43, Nada Ward (January 17, 1995)
image.caption: Earthquake damage around Iwaya Intersection on National Route 43, Nada Ward, 17 January 1995.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: Crime began a long decline under David Dinkins, the city's first black mayor, and kept falling under Rudolph Giuliani, credited with revitalizing Times Square as a Wall Street boom lifted the city.

sources.title: History of New York City (1978–present) - Wikipedia
History of New York City (1978–present) - Wikipedia

image.caption: Times Square at night, July 1997.

cities.name: Mexico City
cities.blurb: Residents won the right to elect their own government in 1997, and Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas became the city's first elected mayor; by then Mexico City was infamous as one of the world's most polluted cities.

image.description: A trolleybus on STE's line A (Eje Central), loading at the Tasqueña terminus, in southern Mexico City and across the street from Tasqueña metro station. The vehicle was built in 1985 by MASA.
image.caption: A trolleybus on line A (Eje Central) at the Tasqueña terminus in southern Mexico City, 15 March 1990.

cities.name: São Paulo
cities.blurb: In 1992 the Tietê Project began a costly, ultimately failed effort to clean Brazil's most polluted river, and from 1996 vehicle restrictions tried to curb winter smog; the Gay Pride Parade began in 1997.

image.credit: Own work. I took the picture.
image.description: Paulista Avenue, the main financial center of São Paulo. A bus stop near MASP - the São Paulo art museum. When I took this picture, the museum had expositions exhibiting artifacts related to Monet, Michelangelo, Portinari and Botero. September 1997.
image.caption: A bus stop on Paulista Avenue near the São Paulo Museum of Art, September 1997.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: Governor Shintaro Ishihara, elected in 1999, attacked the city's debt with spending cuts and a hotel tax, while Roppongi Hills and the Midtown Tower, Tokyo's tallest building on completion in 2007, reshaped the skyline.

image.file: 20031207 7 Desember Roppongi Hills Roppongi Tokyo Japan.jpg
image.description: Roppongi Hills Mori Tower
image.caption: Roppongi Hills Mori Tower, photographed 7 December 2003.

cities.name: Osaka
cities.blurb: Universal Studios Japan, the first Universal theme park outside the United States, opened in Osaka in March 2001; that July, Osaka's bid for the 2008 Olympics was eliminated in the first round.

image.description: Universal Studios JapanPhoto by momopyJuly 2006
image.caption: Universal Studios Japan in July 2006, during its fifth-anniversary year.

cities.name: Mexico City
cities.blurb: From the early 2000s the government and a business group led by Carlos Slim bought and restored centuries-old buildings in the historic centre, replacing drainage, restoring façades and pedestrianizing streets.

image.description: Motolinía Street in the Centro Historico of Mexico City. This section by Tacuba Street is open only to pedestrians
image.caption: A pedestrianized stretch of Motolinía Street in the historic centre of Mexico City, September 2008.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: On 11 September 2001 hijacked airliners destroyed the Twin Towers, spreading toxic debris across Lower Manhattan; under Mayor Michael Bloomberg, a wave of building projects then reshaped large parts of the city.

sources.title: History of New York City (1978–present) - Wikipedia
History of New York City (1978–present) - Wikipedia

image.caption: Smoke rising from the World Trade Center towers in Lower Manhattan, 11 September 2001.

cities.name: São Paulo
cities.blurb: The 2007 Clean City Law stripped billboards and giant advertising panels from the streets, and between 2000 and 2010 the city cut its homicide rate by 78 percent.

image.description: Av. Ibirapuera depois da lei Cidade Limpa
image.caption: Avenida Ibirapuera after the Clean City Law took effect, March 2008.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: The March 2011 Tōhoku earthquake shook Tokyo, liquefying reclaimed land and bringing rolling blackouts; the 634-metre Tokyo Skytree, Japan's tallest structure, was completed that year.

image.description: Tokyo Skytree in 2014
image.caption: Tokyo Skytree, photographed 26 December 2014.

cities.name: Delhi
cities.blurb: Delhi hosted the 2010 Commonwealth Games, the largest sporting event ever held in India, and opened a new airport terminal; in 2013 the new Aam Aadmi Party ousted Congress from the city government.

image.file: Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium CWG opening ceremony.jpg
image.description: The Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, the main stadium for the Delhi Commonwealth Games 2010. Photo was taken on the night of the opening ceremony; security forces can be seen in the foreground.
image.caption: Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on the night of the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony, 3 October 2010.

cities.name: Shanghai
cities.blurb: Twenty years after Pudong was opened for development, it hosted the main venues of Expo 2010; in 2013 Shanghai launched mainland China's first free-trade zone, and the Shanghai Tower, China's tallest building, was completed in 2015.

image.file: Expo 2010 Shanghai flags and China Pavilion.jpg
image.description: South entrance of Expo 2010 Shanghai, near the Expo Boulevard
image.caption: The south entrance of Expo 2010 Shanghai, with the China Pavilion, 20 May 2010.

cities.name: Mexico City
cities.blurb: On 29 January 2016 the Federal District was renamed Ciudad de México, gaining state-like autonomy and boroughs headed by mayors; its own constitution was ratified in 2017.

image.description: Paseo de la Reforma seen from Chapultepec Castle
image.caption: Paseo de la Reforma seen from Chapultepec Castle, 11 January 2014.

cities.name: São Paulo
cities.blurb: The new Arena Corinthians in Itaquera hosted the opening match of the 2014 FIFA World Cup, and in 2015 a major drought led several cities in the state to ration water.

image.description: Fifa World Cup 2014 Opening Ceremony
image.caption: The 2014 FIFA World Cup opening ceremony at Arena Corinthians, 12 June 2014.

snapshots.label: 2020 (projection)

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: The COVID-19 pandemic postponed the 2020 Olympics by a year; they finally opened in July 2021 with spectators banned, and were the most expensive Games held up to that time.

image.file: Drones durante a abertura das Olimpíadas de Tóquio.jpg
image.description: Dezenas de drones formam o Globo Terrestre no Estádio Olímpico de Tóquio.
image.caption: Drones forming a globe over the Olympic Stadium at the opening of the Tokyo Olympics, 23 July 2021.

cities.name: Delhi
cities.blurb: In February 2020 protests over the Citizenship Amendment Act turned into Delhi's worst communal violence in decades in the city's northeast, and its air remained among the most polluted of any city on Earth.

image.description: This is the picture of burnt shops at Shiv Vihar.
image.caption: Burnt shops in Shiv Vihar, northeast Delhi, after the riots, 4 March 2020.

cities.name: Shanghai
cities.blurb: A large COVID-19 outbreak in 2022 led the government to lock down the entire city from 5 April to 1 June, causing widespread food shortages as supply chains broke down.

image.description: Empty streets after lifting Covid-19 restriction
image.caption: Quiet streets on West Nanjing Road after COVID-19 restrictions were lifted, 29 July 2022.

cities.name: São Paulo
cities.blurb: Homelessness rose by almost a third in the two years to 2021, having doubled over twenty years, even as the city was rated Brazil's least lethal capital in the 2023 public security yearbook.

image.file: Sao Paulo Brazil Skyline Aerial, December 2024.jpg
image.description: Drone photo of Sao Paulo skyline, taken from above Parque da Aclimação
image.caption: Drone view of the São Paulo skyline from above Parque da Aclimação, 2 December 2024.

cities.name: Mexico City
cities.blurb: Under head of government Claudia Sheinbaum, the city opened its Cablebús cable-car network in 2021 to serve hillside neighbourhoods, and a second airport, Felipe Ángeles, opened to the north in 2022.

image.artist: Jefatura de Gobierno de la Ciudad de México / Gobierno de la Ciudad de México
image.description: Inaugura Jefa de Gobierno Antena Tlalpexco-Campos Revolución de la Línea 1 de Cablebús en Cuautepec
image.caption: Inauguration of a station on Line 1 of the Cablebús in Cuautepec, 4 March 2021.

snapshots.note: The 2020 and 2025 figures are projections published in the UN's 2018 revision of World Urbanization Prospects, which also projected that Delhi would overtake Tokyo as the most populous city around 2028.

noteSources.title: 2018 Revision of World Urbanization Prospects - UN DESA

snapshots.label: 2025 (projection)

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: Governor Yuriko Koike, first elected in 2016, won a third term in 2024, and her government's Tokyo Green Biz Project, launched in 2023, aims to preserve and expand the city's greenery over the next century.

image.description: A high-angle night photograph of Tokyo, Japan. The Tokyo Tower is prominently illuminated in its traditional orange "Landmark Light." To the left, several modern skyscrapers are visible, including the Azabudai Hills Mori JP Tower and the Roppongi Hills Mori Tower. The foreground and background are filled with a dense grid of lower-rise buildings and residential blocks, creating a tapestry of urban lights. The atmosphere is clear, showing the vast scale of the metropolis at night. Taken from the 35th floor of Shibuya Stream
image.caption: Tokyo at night with the illuminated Tokyo Tower, 3 December 2025.

cities.name: Delhi
cities.blurb: The BJP won an outright majority in the 2025 assembly elections, ending a decade of Aam Aadmi Party government, while the World Air Quality Report 2024 again named Delhi the world's most polluted capital.

cities.name: Shanghai
cities.blurb: Pudong, opened for development in 1990, produced about a third of Shanghai's economy by 2025, and its international airport had become the busiest in China.

image.description: Aerial view of Pudong Airport
image.caption: Aerial view of Shanghai Pudong International Airport, 3 October 2024.

cities.name: Dhaka
cities.blurb: Student protests over government job quotas grew into the July Uprising of 2024; on 5 August, as protesters marched on Dhaka, Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina resigned. The city's first metro line had opened in 2022.

image.file: The victory celebration of Bangladeshi student's one point movement.jpg
image.description: Victory march by protesters after the resignation of Sheikh Hasina in 2024.
image.caption: Protesters celebrating at Shahbag, Dhaka, after Sheikh Hasina's resignation, 5 August 2024.

cities.name: Cairo
cities.blurb: Ministries began moving to the New Administrative Capital east of New Cairo, inaugurated as the seat of government in 2024, and the Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids officially opened on 1 November 2025.

image.file: View of Pyramids of Giza from Grand Egyptian Museum.jpg
image.description: View of Pyramids of Giza from Grand Egyptian Museum
image.caption: The Giza pyramids seen from the Grand Egyptian Museum, 8 March 2024.

snapshots.note: These are 2018 projections. The UN's 2025 revision measures every city with one uniform grid-based definition (Degree of Urbanisation), under which Jakarta ranks first, Dhaka second and Tokyo third.
